newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek M3 sends worrisome inflation signals - bankers.
newsitem.headline: Greek M3 sends worrisome inflation signals - bankers.

text.p: Greek bankers were concerned over prospects for an inflation surge in coming months after a recent pickup in M3 growth, but some doubted the monetary aggregate was a reliable indicator of future inflationary pressures.
Year-over year, May M3 grew a provisional 15.5 percent from April's revised 14.4 percent.

"It is not a good signal for inflation that M3 is growing at such a fast pace," said a senior dealer at a private bank. "You do not have to be a monetarist to believe that there is a link between inflation and the money supply."
The central bank attributed the M3 acceleration to investors' continuing to switch from T-bills to bank deposits.
"The finance ministry's policy of deep rate cuts on government securities has discouraged some investors from buying into T-bills," said an economist at a foreign bank.
The gross rate on the 12-month T-bill stands at 9.60 percent, down from 11.20 percent in early January. A 7.5-percent withholding tax on interest also took effect on January 1.
But some economists said the M3 acceleration alone was not a reliable indicator of future inflationary pressures because its velocity was unstable.
Velocity refers to the number of times the money stock is turned over in a year. When velocity is unstable, some doubt if controlling M3 can keep a rein on inflation.
A monetary aggregate has to have stable and predictable effects on the economy and be controlled by the monetary authorities to be chosen as a target.
"There is some informational content in M3 about future inflation, but its income velocity is unstable," said economics professor and conservative New Democracy party deputy George Alogoskoufis.
Empirical studies show a loose link between M3 growth and inflation, and it takes between six and 12 months before M3 developments show up in inflation, said Alogoskoufis.
Analysts also questioned the usefulness of M3-targeting in the face of financial innovations over the last few years.
M3 does not include shares of money market and fixed-income funds that have mushroomed in the last few years, accounting for over 90 percent of the mutual fund industry's total assets.
It also does not take into account stripped coupons of FRNs and the popular synthetic swaps.
The Bank of Greece uses M3 and the exchange rate as intermediate policy targets to reduce inflation to 4.5 percent at end-97 and below 3.0 percent at end-98.
Alogoskoufis, who was also chairman of the council of economic advisors in the last conservative government, favoured nominal GDP targeting. But GDP data are not readily available.
May consumer price inflation fell to 5.4 percent year-on-year from April's 5.9 percent. But May's core rate, exculding volatile food and energy prices, rose to 7.6 percent from April's 7.4 percent.
The Bank of Greece has set an end-97 target for M3 growth between 6.0 and 9.0 percent and has said it wants the drachma to be stable versus major currencies making up the ecu this year.
The central bank also monitors the broader M4 money supply and credit expansion to the private and public sector.
May M4 grew provisionally by 8.6 percent year-on-year from April's revised 9.1 percent, within the central bank's 8.0-11.0 percent zone and in line of reaching year-end inflation goals.
April credit growth was 9.3 percent year-on-year from March's 8.2 percent, above the central bank's 4.0-6.0 percent zone. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
